author: KaleSalen
title: Amazing casual game despite misleading ads… but it has limits
text: • Summary • Advertisements make this look like a puzzle or story-choice game, but Gossip Harbor is primarily a merging game. You have to drag ingredients around a board to create new dishes. It’s enjoyable at first, but becomes repetitive over time. As you level up and unlock more dishes (and the x2 option), it takes more energy, which eventually slows progress and forces you to wait two hours to get full. You only experience the story & decorating element after serving customers and getting enough money. •• It’s best to look at the last 3 previews to get a solid idea of what the game offers, and not the rest. ——————••—————— • Plot • The game truly shines with its story. It’s engaging, mysterious, and keeps you hooked. The characters are interesting, the presentation feels genuine, and the overall storytelling is impressive. ——————••—————— • Decoration • The decoration system starts out fun but gradually feels limited (only 3 options). You are given the option to choose between the other options by tapping & holding the furniture (if available) Remember, the only way to decorate is to progress the game and serve customers! ——————••—————— • Transactions • In-app purchases are reasonably priced for what they offer (to spenders), but they’re not very useful for casual gameplay since it (⚡️) disappears quickly. Because of this, spending money can feel unnecessary and may even encourage unhealthy spending habits. Not to mention the length of each event — some are only a few hours while others are days — and luck probability. •• Game has a habit of pushing bundles out, from starter packs, to level packs. Otherwise, it doesn’t constantly shove in-app purchases at your face. ——————••—————— Conclusion: ✅ Good for casual players ❎ Not ideal for anyone wanting deep, long-term gameplay due to the limited ⚡️ system.

text: This game starts out fun, but very quickly it becomes obvious that it is designed to make players spend a lot of money. It feels like the game intentionally blocks your progress so you feel forced to pay. Even small actions start to require more and more resources, which makes it frustrating. What’s worse is that the in-app purchases are quite expensive, and even after spending money, it doesn’t feel like you get enough value. You can easily spend a lot and still feel stuck in the game. Overall, the game feels less like entertainment and more like a money trap. Unless you are willing to spend a lot of money regularly, it becomes very difficult to enjoy the game.

author: MinaA*
title: Not Enough Energy
text: I really love this game, it’s so fun and I truly enjoy playing it. However, I am currently on level 50 and I’m getting sick of how much energy bolts I need to simply finish 1 order. It takes 2 minutes to generate 1 energy bolt and it wont let you save more than a 100 bolts at a time, so you have to play every 3 hours to not waste energy bolts. It takes 1200 bolts to make the lobster dish, and since I only get 100 bolts max I literally have to play for 2-4 days to make it. This actually sucks, I really liked this game but it’s starting to get on my nerves so much. I hope that they change it and make it easier for us to play the game, because the game is really fun but I also don’t have the patience or time to keep checking every few hours to not waste the energy I’m given. Things that can help improve the game: 1. Being allowed to save more than a 100 energy bolts at a time (should be at least 200-300) 2. Making it cheaper to purchase dishes with our diamonds (560 diamonds for a crab dish is mental, I can make $560 irl faster than 560 diamonds in the game) 3. Allow us to choose what to generate because why do I need to generate 50 cups of coffee just so I can get 1 teacup, we should be able to choose what we want the machine to generate instead of having to waste all that time and bolts to generate a bloody teapot. Thank you and have a nice day.

author: yosif wissam
title: Suggestion
text: This game is really fun and addictive. I enjoy the gameplay, the story, and the overall design—it keeps me coming back. However, there is one major issue that makes it feel unfair. As you progress to higher levels, the tasks become much harder and require a lot more energy, sometimes up to 500 energy to complete a single order. Despite that, the game still limits you to only 100 energy, which is not enough to do anything meaningful at higher levels. On top of that, the energy prices are quite expensive. Because of this, I find myself spending money on the game almost every week just to keep playing, which shouldn’t be necessary to enjoy the experience. I think the game should increase the maximum energy as players level up. For example, it could go up to 200 or more over time. Since the game becomes more challenging, the energy system should also scale with progression. Right now, 100 energy is simply not enough for advanced levels. It would also be great if the game added rewards like unlimited energy for 10–15 minutes after reaching certain goals. Features like this would make the game more enjoyable and fair, and they definitely need more development. Overall, it’s a great and enjoyable game, but these issues really need improvement to make the experience fair for players.

text: I downloaded Gossip Harbor based on the ads, and honestly, it’s incredibly misleading. The advertisements make it look like a completely different game—fun, interactive, and story-driven in a way that just isn’t reflected in the actual gameplay. What you get instead feels repetitive and nowhere near as engaging as what’s being promoted. Even more frustrating is how aggressively the game pushes in-app purchases. If you want to make any real progress or actually enjoy playing, you’re basically forced to spend money—often a lot of it. Energy runs out quickly, rewards are minimal, and progress slows to a crawl unless you pay. Overall, it feels like a bait-and-switch. The ads draw you in with something that doesn’t exist, and the game itself is heavily monetized to the point where it’s more frustrating than fun. Definitely not worth the download unless you’re prepared to spend money constantly.

text: This game is really fun and enjoyable, especially since it doesn’t have ads,that’s honestly my favorite part. However, I think the developers could improve the energy system. For example, it would be nice if players received free energy whenever a new day starts. Also, the energy cap is only 100, while many items require 700+ energy to create, which makes progression feel a bit too slow. Another issue is that the game constantly caps your energy at 100, which pushes players to spend money for more energy. I understand that in-app purchases are part of how games make money, and at first the deals were pretty reasonable, around $2–$3 or even $8.99. But as I progressed to higher levels, the game only started offering expensive bundles like $19 or $29, which feels a bit unfair and discouraging for players who just want to enjoy the game casually.

As a queer Asian man myself I was genuinely shocked. The main character being a Hispanic single mother too, and the young girl wanting to be an astronaut… there is so much positivity and genuine struggles posed in this story in such a digestible way, that I was not expecting for a merge and match game. I haven’t seen media make diversity so normalized in a while, and was incredibly pleasantly surprised to see it here. Besides that, it’s just a fun game with no advertisements and no tricks. Amazing, highly recommend!

author: Anonymous:)101
title: Real/honest review
text: I rarely leave reviews, but I felt this one was worth writing. First, the game is nothing like the ads. To be fair, the game itself is enjoyable, but the marketing is misleading. The ads portray gameplay that simply doesn’t exist. If anything, the mechanics shown in the ads would make excellent optional side activities or mini games, and I would genuinely enjoy seeing them added. My second concern is far more significant. This is a game marketed toward children (13+), yet it includes romantic and gender-identity themes that I do not believe belong in children’s entertainment. For example, there is a scene in which Sam, a male character, makes flirtatious advances toward a male police officer, as well as the inclusion of a non-binary character using they/them pronouns. I understand that the developers may view this as an effort to promote inclusivity. However, children’s games should remain focused on gameplay rather than introducing social or ideological topics that are unrelated to the game’s purpose. Children do not need these themes woven into their entertainment, especially when they are too young to fully understand them. There is a clear difference between representing a diverse audience and deliberately incorporating contemporary social messaging into media designed for children/teens. I believe children’s games should prioritize age-appropriate storytelling and entertainment over advancing cultural or political viewpoints. Overall, the gameplay is enjoyable, but the misleading advertising and the unnecessary inclusion of these themes significantly diminish the experience.

text: Nothing special. There are countless other games very similar, and it’s nothing like the game shown in the ads. Sure, there are no forced ads, but it’s still an endless merge game built around time-locked progression and wildly overpriced microtransactions. Not the game the ads promised. At all. If you want the details: The game lets you progress rapidly at first, constantly rewarding you to get you invested. Then everything slows to a crawl until you’re waiting absurd amounts of time to make any progress. That’s the business model: create impatience, then sell overpriced gems and coins for essentially time-skips as the solution. These games are intentionally designed to push players toward spending money. They create artificial obstacles and delays, then charge you to remove them. They’re just entertaining enough to keep you coming back, but deliberately frustrating enough that paying starts to feel like the easiest option. Eventually you realize you’re not paying for more fun, you’re only paying to remove problems the developers intentionally created. And they almost got me. Nice try. Oh and let’s not even get started on how Apple does not have a review interface to allow you to see anything other than what they deem “Most Helpful”. But what do we expect from a company that is heavily incentivized to, and has a long history of, profit maximizing over their customers interests.

After a few purchases, the targets increased to 240, then 280 after I failed a week. Now I’m expected to complete 4,500 merges, earn 300 Good Reviews, collect 24,000 coins, and gather 350 cards in a single week. For a normal player, that’s simply unrealistic unless you’re spending constantly. What disappointed me the most was customer support. I reached out to explain that the weekly requirements felt impossible. The response was basically, “We’ll pass your feedback to the developers.” Instead of seeing any improvement, the goals became even harder afterward. I know that may have been a coincidence, but it honestly left me feeling like loyal, paying players are being pushed away rather than rewarded. This is still a genuinely good game with beautiful graphics and no intrusive ads, which is why this is so disappointing. I don’t mind a challenge, but the weekly events should reward dedication—not make players feel punished for supporting the game or for missing a week. Unless the progression and event balancing are made fairer, I can’t recommend spending money on this game.

author: BK don’t do it
title: It Doesn’t Reward Your Curiosity—It Monetizes It
text: After reaching Level 107, Day 126, and spending over $1,000, I can honestly say Gossip Harbor is one of the most aggressively monetized mobile games I’ve ever played. The merge gameplay is enjoyable, and the original Gnome mystery pulled me in. Unfortunately, that’s where the satisfying storytelling ends. The biggest problem isn’t the cost—it’s the lack of payoff. After the original Gnome storyline, the game continually introduces new mysteries before resolving the old ones. Characters disappear, secrets pile up, relationships change, and every story scene teases answers without actually providing them. Instead of delivering satisfying conclusions, the game keeps moving the finish line. Progress is also buried behind layer after layer of artificial delays. Energy runs out, generators recharge, high-level merge chains become increasingly tedious, coins are required to unlock story chores, and events constantly encourage spending on bundles, gems, passes, and special offers. If you want to experience the story at a reasonable pace, the game repeatedly nudges you toward your wallet. Even worse, the game’s own story recap stops at Day 50, while I reached Day 126. If the developers expect players to follow a complex mystery spanning well over 100 story days, they should at least provide a recap that keeps up. Looking back at my Apple purchase history was eye-opening. I didn’t spend over $1,000 because the game delivered $1,000 worth of content. I spent it speeding through artificial roadblocks, only to receive another small piece of dialogue that usually created more questions than answers. Gossip Harbor isn’t a bad game. It has charm, polished artwork, and an engaging premise. But it relies too heavily on stretching out the story and monetizing player curiosity rather than rewarding it. I don’t mind paying for a good game. I do mind paying over and over just to keep chasing answers that never seem to come. My rating: 2 out of 5 stars. The gameplay is fun, but the storytelling and monetization eventually turn curiosity into frustration.

If you need to advertise your own games every few seconds, fine—but then don’t advertise the game as “AD-FREE.” Be honest with players about what they are downloading. “Free” and “ad-free” are two completely different promises. This game delivers neither the experience shown in the advertisement nor the ad-free experience it claims to provide. Stop misleading people with advertisements that the actual game doesn’t live up to. It’s frustrating, annoying, and makes it very difficult to trust anything else the developer claims.

author: SweetGiraffe11
title: Disappointed in What This Game Has Become
text: I used to absolutely love Gossip Harbor. It was one of my go-to games, and I still like the game itself, but the balance has shifted so far toward monetization that it just isn’t as enjoyable anymore. Originally, there were two daily gifts you could collect for free. Then they added a third, made the piggy bank cost diamonds, and let you watch an ad for the energy box. I honestly didn’t mind that setup at all. I rarely depended on the piggy bank anyway, and watching an ad for extra energy felt like a fair trade. Now the only truly free daily gift is a tiny box that is mostly coins and may give you a couple pieces of energy. Even the actual energy box costs diamonds now, and when you do spend the diamonds on it, it doesn’t even fully recharge your energy anymore. That would be less frustrating if the energy demands in the game had stayed reasonable, but they haven’t. You have to spend energy to generate items and then merge them repeatedly to make the higher-level items required for orders. As you progress, you increasingly get several orders at once asking for very high-level or max-level items. You can burn through all of your energy making those items and still barely make a dent. The events are where it becomes especially noticeable. I can play for multiple days, miss completing several events because I simply cannot generate enough energy, and still not unlock another piece of the story. At that point it stops feeling like normal progression and starts feeling artificially slowed unless you spend diamonds or real money. I’ve also had glitches lately where I open a chest, receive energy as a reward, and then the energy never actually gets added to my balance. I still enjoy Gossip Harbor, which is why this is disappointing. I haven’t stopped playing, but it is no longer the game I automatically open when I have a few minutes to relax. I really wish the developers would bring back the balance the game used to have, where spending money felt optional and simply playing the game still felt rewarding.

author: Doodlebug’s mom
title: It’s not what’s advertised but it is a lot of fun
text: The ads that you see where you choose to fix a broken window or light a fire to determine if the characters survive? That’s not what this is. But it’s still a great game. I have been playing daily for many months. What it is: You choose from breads, coffees, pool floaties, seashells, etc. and use energy to produce small items. Then you match small items to make big ones. For example, two buns make a baguette, two baguettes make a loaf of sliced bread, etc. Merge items to fill customer orders, earning gold, jewels, and other items. Spend your gold to upgrade your restaurant and, ultimately, your entire property. As you do so a story unfolds where you get to know characters, build relationships, and read an unfolding mystery. Your choices are mostly “do you want this decoration in blue, yellow, or pink?” You do not choose the course of the story at all. Though I was disappointed at first that it’s not the game I thought it was, I quickly grew to love it. Here’s why: 1. Rhythm. Producing and merging items give me a nice dopamine hit by way of the rhythm that unfolds in the process. 2. Variety. There are tons of side quests. In the beginning I stuck to the primary function, but my adhd brain loves all of the extras. 3. Self-limiting. Energy accumulates over time, about one point every couple-few minutes. It maxes at 100 points, unless you are actively reaching goals that give you more. Unlike social media’s endless scroll, this produces stopping points that let me take my dopamine hit and then get back to work. 4. Truly free, truly ad-free. If you choose to stick to the imposed limits you can pop in and out of the game at intervals and play with your accumulated energy. You have options to purchase extras, either by watching ads or paying money, but neither is a requirement in order to play the game. The only drawback for me is the eleventy-bajillion pop-ups when I first open the game, or when I switch between tasks. I understand that the point of this work is for the producers to make a profit so I don’t fret about it. The side-quests are often time-limited. You’ll find it very-difficult-to-impossible to complete them without paying money. I don’t begrudge anyone their need to make a living, and I have certain places where I watch the ads in order to earn extras. You do what suits you. This really is a great game, I don’t understand the need to promote it with images and activities that aren’t in the actual game.

title: Fun, but not "that game"
text: This game is fun, but it's not the advertised game as it claims to be. Certain elements are, like being (almost) ad-free (except for optimal things like more energy and such) and the mom is a divorcée. The divorce happens because Quinn finds her husband Colin surrounded by other women at a casino, but she's not unhoused or living in squalor, she doesn't have to give a baby up for adoption--in fact, she doesn't have a baby at all--and you don't use merging to help her rebuild her home. Instead, you have to rebuild her restaurant after people set fire to it, which you find out is related to food poisonings that happened there. In the process, you try to find out who set fire to it and who was behind the poisoning. I did not get that far to find out because, while the game is fun, the lying got to me. That said, if you don't mind that it's not the game it pretends to be, then it's a good game to play.

I don’t generally like merge games, but was willing to give it a try in hopes it did match the ads, and because it highlighted the story as a key feature. The story makes no sense, to a degree that it feels like they changed their minds halfway through development about what they wanted the story to be, and then didn’t update all the dialogue to match the new direction. Didn’t we start by saying this was her restaurant she was running with her husband, that was then destroyed by rioters (wtf) after people were literally poisoned there? Why does she keep having to explain to people that she owns the restaurant with her husband, and doing things like introducing her daughter to her “best friend?” Haven’t they been living in this town already? Seems like the story was originally the classic moving back to your hometown and inheriting a dilapidated building, but for some reason they changed it to sabotage and possible attempted murder. In any case, it’s not at all like the ads (shocker). I played for a while anyway, but around the time the 8th or 9th concurrent “special event” popped up on the side of the screen, I realized I wasn’t actually having any fun. I was content to just delete it, but in the hour and a half total I’ve spent since then playing other games, I’ve gotten easily a dozen of their disingenuous and/or bizarrely emotionally manipulative ads telling me how this game is the one I’ve been searching for. author: JKT1234567890
title: Aggressive monetization
text: The graphics are great, the game is well designed, and I really enjoy the variety of events and mini-games. I also appreciate that there are no ads. Unfortunately, the aggressive monetization takes away a lot of the enjoyment. Many limited-time events seem intentionally designed so that regular energy regeneration and normal gameplay are simply not enough to complete them within the given time. You can make some progress for free, but if you want to actually finish the event and earn the main reward, you are constantly pushed toward buying diamonds, coins, energy, or one of the many packages being offered. I understand that mobile games need to make money, but there should be a reasonable balance. Players who spend time playing consistently should still have a realistic chance to complete events without having to spend significant amounts of money every time. It’s disappointing because this could be a really enjoyable game. The graphics and content deserve more than one star, but the excessive pay-to-progress design does not.

author: Amerissá
title: Age verification
text: I love this game. It's the only game that's survived my mass app deletions over the years, but now I'm being asked to verify my age through k-ID by uploading my driver's license or a photo of my face. I'm already signed in through Apple to protect my account and game progress. Surely there should be a way to use an existing, trusted account or another verification method rather than requiring players to submit sensitive personal information. I understand that there may be legal or regulatory requirements the developers need to follow. However, I live in GA in the US, and I haven't found a law that requires players of a mobile game like this to upload their ID or face. If this is legally required, please explain which law applies. I'm also uncomfortable being directed to a third-party website that assures me my information isn't retained. That's a promise I'm expected to trust with my government-issued identification or facial image, and I don't feel comfortable taking that risk just to play a mobile game. I love Gossip Harbor, which makes this especially disappointing. But I'm not uploading my driver's license or face to continue playing. Please offer players a less intrusive way to verify their age and a clear explanation of why this information is necessary.

author: MiyoMeOhMy
title: GIVE ME A REFUND
text: It’s NOT as advertised. The mom and kid are NOT poor and dirty in tattered clothing. Besides that, the plot is written like a teen wrote it. Our protag is weird and wishy washy and has the attention span of a goldfish. I could forgive all of that because the merging aspect is not as dumb as other merge games. Cupcake becomes a small cake becomes a large cake and then a larger cake. Makes sense. Unlike other games, the merging makes sense. I could forgive that the events do not give you enough time to finish them (for free anyway.) And I could forgive that there is only 100 energy and ONLY ever 100 energy allowed to be recharged because you can somewhat manage to play well for a while. What I CANNOT forgive is that this game is impossible to play the longer you play it. The 100 energy limit is absolutely awful for higher levels— you barely have enough to start any order cuz the orders become impossibly larger. And the game doesn’t throw you much freebies that you can merge to help you reach say, the giant Lvl 10 lobster meal or whatever because they give you the small Lvl 1-5 things. The rewards for most things are hardly worth the effort too for mini games and mini events! I feel like I need at least 200 energy to get anywhere at the game level I’m at: 30+. I’ve even spent money a little to get farther in events and not even that helps— I wish I had a refund cuz I feel dumb for thinking those little packs would get me far into any event. The game basically begs you to pay money at higher levels and I don’t forgive any of this stuff. I’m starting to regret playing it— and I feel like starting over itself isn’t a good idea either. No wins here at all. Smh. I hate how I have like 8 gems, unlocked the bonus reward thing, and I have mostly nothing to show for it. Btw don’t do the weird Story Mode quests— they are a waste of energy and a waste of time. The rewards suck! And merging to the rocketship or dog or whatever takes so long that the tiny reward won’t be worth it. Overall, I wish I had my time and money back. I liked the merging and yes there is no ads but that’s it. Ugh. LIKE. I WANT A FULL REFUND BRO.

title: It’s ok
text: There was a time where you’d get items to merge and they’d pop out another item of the next level in an ice cube. Say you combine two level 7 sandwiches and sometimes you get a random level 8 sandwich from it. This level 8 sandwich would be in a cube. That cube with a level 8 sandwich had approximately 5 minutes or so before it dissolved and turned into a coin. Within that time frame, if you can level another sandwich to level 8 and combine them together, it would give you an instant level 9 sandwich. A latest update flipped that and now it turns into a lower level item instead of the next level up. So when you combine a level 7 item, now you’ll get a lower level item of 6 instead of 8. It’s the little things that they do that purposely slows down your progress, I don’t purchase anything from this game anymore, I used to do the monthly booster pass, not anymore. You can get everything for free in this game with just normal play, the game is designed to make you buy diamonds progress faster, it’s not really necessary at all to spend any money on this game and I wouldn’t recommend playing this game because of the changes the developers have made.
